sections.title: Routing Fundamentals
sections.content:
A router forwards packets between networks using the destination IP and its routing table. For each packet it finds the most specific match (longest prefix) and sends it out the matching next hop/interface.
How entries get into the table:
Directly connected — networks on the router's own interfaces.
Static routes — manually configured; precise and low-overhead, but don't adapt to changes. A default route (0.0.0.0/0) is a static catch-all pointing to the gateway of last resort.
Dynamic routes — learned from a routing protocol; adapt automatically as the network changes.
Administrative distance (AD) ranks trust when multiple sources offer a route: Connected 0, Static 1, eBGP 20, OSPF 110, RIP 120. Lower AD wins. Within one protocol, a metric picks the best path.
exam_tips: Longest prefix match wins: a /30 route beats a /24 for an address inside it.
Lower administrative distance = more trusted source. Static (1) beats OSPF (110) beats RIP (120).
0.0.0.0/0 is the default route — used when nothing more specific matches.

sections.title: Dynamic Routing Protocols
sections.content:
Interior Gateway Protocols (within one organization):
RIP — distance-vector, metric = hop count (max 15). Simple, slow to converge, legacy.
OSPF — link-state, metric = cost (based on bandwidth). Fast convergence, scalable, uses areas. The common enterprise IGP.
EIGRP — Cisco's advanced distance-vector (hybrid), fast convergence.
Exterior Gateway Protocol (between organizations / the internet):
BGP — path-vector, the routing protocol of the internet; chooses paths by policy across autonomous systems (AS).
Distance-vector (RIP) shares its whole table with neighbors ('routing by rumor'); link-state (OSPF) builds a full map of the network and runs shortest-path first (Dijkstra).
exam_tips: OSPF = link-state, cost metric, areas. RIP = distance-vector, hop-count, max 15 hops.
BGP is the internet's routing protocol — path-vector, between autonomous systems.

sections.title: NAT & Bandwidth Management
sections.content:
NAT (Network Address Translation) lets many private hosts share public IPs.
Static NAT — one-to-one private-to-public mapping.
Dynamic NAT — maps from a pool.
PAT (overload) — many private hosts to ONE public IP, distinguished by port number. This is what home/office routers do.
Bandwidth & traffic management:
QoS (Quality of Service) — prioritizes latency-sensitive traffic (VoIP, video) using marking (DSCP/CoS), queuing, and policing/shaping.
Traffic shaping buffers and smooths bursts; policing drops/remarks traffic over a limit.
A 'default gateway' is the router a host sends off-subnet traffic to.
exam_tips: PAT (NAT overload) maps many private IPs to one public IP using port numbers — the home-router default.
QoS prioritizes real-time traffic (VoIP/video); mark with DSCP, then queue/shape.

concept_cards.hook: A ranking of how trustworthy a route source is (Connected 0, Static 1, OSPF 110, RIP 120). The lowest AD wins when sources conflict.
The router forwards using the most specific (longest subnet mask) matching route in its table.
0.0.0.0/0 — the catch-all route used when no more specific entry matches; points to the gateway of last resort.
A link-state interior gateway protocol that builds a full topology map and picks paths by cost (bandwidth). Fast-converging and scalable with areas.
Border Gateway Protocol — the path-vector routing protocol of the internet, exchanging routes between autonomous systems by policy.
Port Address Translation — maps many private IPs to a single public IP, keeping sessions separate by port number.
Quality of Service — prioritizing delay-sensitive traffic (VoIP/video) through marking (DSCP), queuing, shaping, and policing.
Distance-vector (RIP) shares its whole table with neighbors by hop count; link-state (OSPF) maps the whole network and runs shortest-path-first.

practice_questions.q: A route to 10.1.1.0/24 exists via both OSPF and a static route. Which is installed?
practice_questions.explanation: Lower administrative distance wins; static (1) beats OSPF (110).

practice_questions.q: Which routing protocol has a maximum hop count of 15?
practice_questions.explanation: RIP counts hops with 16 meaning unreachable, so 15 is the maximum usable.

practice_questions.q: A router receives a packet matching both a /24 and a /26 route. Which does it use?
practice_questions.explanation: Routers always use the most specific (longest prefix) matching route.

practice_questions.q: Which NAT type maps many internal hosts to one public IP using port numbers?
practice_questions.explanation: PAT distinguishes many internal sessions behind one public IP by source port.

practice_questions.q: Which protocol would you use to route between two different companies over the internet?
practice_questions.explanation: BGP exchanges routes between autonomous systems and is the internet's routing protocol.

practice_questions.q: Marking traffic with DSCP values is part of which function?
practice_questions.explanation: DSCP marking classifies packets so QoS can prioritize them.

practice_questions.q: Which QoS mechanism buffers and smooths bursts of traffic to a defined rate?
practice_questions.explanation: Shaping buffers excess traffic to smooth it; policing simply drops/remarks over the limit.

practice_questions.q: What address does a host use to reach destinations outside its own subnet?
practice_questions.explanation: Off-subnet traffic is sent to the default gateway (the local router interface).

practice_questions.q: Which describes a link-state routing protocol?
options: Shares its entire table with neighbors by hop count
Builds a full map of the network and runs shortest-path-first
practice_questions.explanation: Link-state protocols (OSPF) compute paths from a complete topology map using Dijkstra's SPF.

practice_questions.q: A static route configured as 0.0.0.0/0 is known as a:
practice_questions.explanation: 0.0.0.0/0 matches any destination and is the default (gateway of last resort) route.
